member.name: T:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.ApplicationIdentity
member.summary: Which of the two applications a credential file belongs to (AR3: each has its own SQL login, so each has its own credential file).
member.remarks:
This selects the DPAPI optionalEntropy value, and that is the whole of its job. Analysis §6.1 is explicit that the entropy is not a security boundary: G18 puts both applications on one machine, ciphertext is decryptable by any process there, and the entropy is a byte array sitting in the other application's own binary. The NTFS ACL is the control.
What the entropy does buy is worth having anyway: a blob sealed for one application fails loudly in the other rather than decrypting into the wrong credential. Copying the loader's secrets.json into the monitor's directory is a plausible operator mistake, and the failure mode without entropy is the monitor connecting to SQL Server as the loader.

member.name: P:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.CredentialBootstrapOptions.LockTimeout
member.summary: How long to wait for another process to finish with the credential file before giving up.
member.remarks:
This must exceed however long validation takes, and validation is a network round trip: a SQL login, or an EPA auth call. The process that wins the lock holds it across that call — it has to, because G5 requires the Encrypted flag to be re-read inside the lock — so the process that loses waits out the winner's entire login, including the winner's connect timeout if the server is slow to answer. Sixty seconds is four times the SQL Server default connect timeout of fifteen, which leaves room for a retry inside the validator.
Set too low, the symptom is not a hang. It is one of the two co-resident applications reporting on the one run per environment where both start at once — the seeding run, under G18, which the plan calls the normal case rather than an edge case.

member.name: P:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.CredentialBootstrapOptions.LockPollInterval
member.summary: How long to wait between attempts to open the file.
member.remarks: There is no file-lock wait primitive on Windows for this: a sharing violation is an error, not a blocking call, so the wait is a poll. Fifty milliseconds is short enough that the loser starts promptly after the winner finishes and long enough that a minute of waiting is about a thousand attempts rather than a spin.

member.name: T:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.CredentialBootstrapper
member.summary: AR4, end to end: read the credential file, prove the credentials work, and — if they were in plaintext — seal them and rewrite the file, once, under an exclusive lock.

remarks.para: This is Analysis §6.1's G5 matrix as one method. Each row is an outcome of and each is reproduced by a test:

item.description: leave the plaintext exactly as it was, report the reason, do not continue
fail fast naming the re-seed procedure; never overwrite, never fall back

item.term: Encrypted: true, decrypts but validation fails
item.description: report the reason, do not continue — the password was rotated upstream
exclusive lock, and the flag is re-read inside it

remarks.para: Why the whole of it happens inside one open handle. The lock is not a separate lock file: it is the credential file itself, opened . Read, decide, and rewrite all go through that handle, which is what makes "re-read and re-check Encrypted inside the lock" true rather than merely intended — there is no window between the check and the write for the other application to seal the file first. Validation happens inside the lock too, which means the loser of the race waits out the winner's network round trip; see .

Why the rewrite is in place, and not the safer-looking temp-file swap. The file's DACL is the only thing standing between the co-resident web application and this application's SQL password (Analysis §6.1, G18: LocalMachine ciphertext is decryptable by any process on the box, and Set-CredentialFileAcl.ps1 writes an explicit deny for the IIS application pool identity). Measured on this project, against a file carrying that deny ACE with inheritance switched off:

description.b: deny ACE gone, inheritance back on
deny ACE gone, inheritance back on

remarks.para: Two of the four obvious ways to rewrite a file silently discard the ACE, and the two that survive are not equally good here: File.Replace preserves the destination's DACL but the temp file it needs is created with the directory's inherited permissions, so for the moment it exists the application pool identity can read the ciphertext out of it. In-place has no second file, cannot lose the DACL, and needs no ACL code of its own.

The cost of in-place is a crash window: a process that dies between the truncate and the flush leaves a file with no recoverable password in it. That is accepted rather than engineered around, because the remedy already exists and is already mandatory — the password is in the password manager (plan §4.2), and re-seeding is the documented response to the far more likely machine rebuild. A test asserts that no sibling file is ever created, so a later refactor to the temp-file form has to argue with a failing test rather than quietly hand the web application a readable copy.

member.name: T:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.CredentialFile
member.summary: The contents of one credential file: the Encrypted flag, the secrets, and everything else the file happens to contain.

remarks.para: Why this is not a deserialized POCO. The file is hand-written by whoever seeds the environment (plan §4.2 step 1) and rewritten in place by the application. Round-tripping it through a class with four properties would silently delete every property the class does not know about — an operator's own note, a key added by a later revision, a setting someone put here rather than in appsettings.json. There is no backup of this file and no source control copy of it, by design. So it is read as a , exactly four properties are touched, and the rest is written back unchanged.

Key lookup is case-insensitive, and a case collision is an error. Operators type "encrypted". Reading one spelling and writing another would leave a file that says both, one of them stale — and the stale one being Encrypted: false over a sealed value is a file that re-seals its own ciphertext on the next run. So a file containing two spellings of the same key is refused rather than guessed at.

What is lost on a rewrite: comments and formatting. Both are accepted on the way in — hand-edited JSON has trailing commas and // notes in it — and neither survives , because does not carry them. Stated in the runbook rather than worked around: the file is normalized the first time the application seals it.

member.name: F:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.CredentialFile.DefaultFileName
member.summary: The file name this class expects, and the reason reloadOnChange never comes up.
member.remarks:
Analysis §6.1 requires reloadOnChange: false on the file the application rewrites, or the web application recycles itself the moment it encrypts its own configuration. This design goes a step further and takes the file out of the configuration system altogether: it is read by this class, not by IConfiguration, so there is no file watcher to disable and no way for a later `AddJsonFile` call to reintroduce one by omitting an argument. The name is deliberately not appsettings*.json, which is what the default host configuration globs.
.gitignore already excludes this exact name, and build/check_gitignore_secrets.py asserts that it does.

member.summary: Proves that credentials work, by using them. Supplied by the application rather than implemented here: RCRAInfo.Core knows nothing about SQL Server or HTTP, and both of the real validators are one of those two things.
member.param: The plaintext credentials to try.

Called before anything is encrypted, on every path — that is G5's first two rows, and the whole of "never encrypt a password that failed validation". It is also called on the already-sealed path, because a password rotated upstream is G5's fourth row and the only way to detect it is to try it.
An implementation is expected to return a rejection rather than throw one. A thrown exception is treated as a rejection too, so a validator that throws on a bad login is not a defect — but its exception message goes to the operator, and an exception from an HTTP stack carries a URI with a query string, which is why AR8 forbids logging one whole (see ).

member.name: M:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.CredentialValidators.All(RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.CredentialValidator[])
member.summary: Runs validators in order and returns the first rejection, or valid if every one accepts.
member.param: The validators, in the order they should run. Order is a decision, not a detail — the loader's SQL login goes first so that an unreachable SQL Server is not reported as a problem with an API Key nobody tried.
member.returns: A validator that requires all of them.

remarks.para: Short-circuiting, and not only for speed. The credential file holds several secrets and the bootstrapper seals all of them together or none, so the first rejection already decides the outcome; running the rest would add a second failure message about a credential that is fine and leave an operator guessing which one to fix.

An empty list is refused rather than treated as valid. "Validate against nothing" is what a misconfigured host produces, and its effect would be to seal every secret in the file without checking any of them — the exact outcome AR4's validation step exists to prevent.

member.name: T:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.DpapiSecretProtector
member.summary: The AR4 mechanism: Windows DPAPI at scope with a per-application optionalEntropy value, Base64 for the file.

remarks.para: Why and not CurrentUser (Analysis §6.1): the two applications run under different identities — a Task Scheduler service account and an IIS application pool. CurrentUser binds the ciphertext to one Windows profile and needs that profile loaded, which is the classic "works interactively, fails when scheduled" failure. LocalMachine is robust under both hosts, and its weakness — any process on the box can decrypt — is answered by the file ACL, not by the scope.

The entropy is derived from a constant, and that is deliberate. It is a fixed string per application, hashed to 32 bytes so the length is uniform. It is not a key, it is not secret, and hardening it would be theatre: it ships inside the binary of the application it belongs to, on the same machine as the ciphertext. See for what it does buy.

The version suffix in each literal exists so that a future decision to change the entropy is forced to be a deliberate, named change. Changing these strings invalidates every sealed file in every environment — the same consequence as a machine rebuild, and it needs the same re-seed visit.

member.name: T:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.ISecretProtector
member.summary: Turns a plaintext secret into a string that can sit in a file, and back again.
member.remarks:
An interface rather than a direct call to for one reason that matters and one that does not.
The reason that matters: G5's third row — Encrypted: true and decryption fails — is the row with the strictest requirement on this code ("never silently overwrite or fall back to plaintext"), and it is the row that in production is caused by a machine rebuild. A test cannot rebuild the machine. It can substitute a protector that throws, and it can also produce the real thing three other ways: tamper with the ciphertext, seal with one application's entropy and open with the other's, or set the flag to true over a value that was never sealed at all. All four are exercised; three of them go through real DPAPI.
The reason that does not matter: portability. Nothing here is expected to run off Windows. G18 puts both applications on Windows Server in all three environments.

member.name: M:RCRAInfo.Core.Credentials.ISecretProtector.Unprotect(System.String)
member.summary: Recovers a secret sealed by .
member.param: The sealed form as read from the file.
member.exception: The value could not be recovered — for any reason, including a value that is not even in the right encoding. One exception type, because the caller's only correct response to every cause is the same: refuse to start and tell the operator to re-seed. An implementation that let a escape instead would reach a catch block written for cryptographic failure and crash with a stack trace rather than the actionable message G5 requires.
